edition.name: Migne, Patrologia Latina (PL 1, Paris 1844), Apologeticus, via Latin Wikisource transcription
edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Augustus imperii formator, ne dominum quidem dici se volebat; et hoc enim dei est cognomen. Dicam plane imperatorem dominum, sed more communi, sed quando non cogor, ut dominum dei vice dicam. Caeterum liber sum illi; dominus enim meus unus est, Deus omnipotens et aeternus, idem qui et ipsius. Qui pater patriae est, quomodo dominus est. Sed est gratius nomen pietatis, quam potestatis; etiam familiae magis patres, quam domini vocantur. Tanto abest, ut imperator deus debeat dici, quod non potest credi non modo turpissima, sed et perniciosa adulatione; tanquam si habens imperatorem, alterum appelles, nonne maximam et inexorabilem offensam contrahes ejus, quem habuisti, etiam ipsi timendam, quem appellasti? Esto religiosus in deum, qui vis illum propitium imperatori. Desine alium Deum colere vel credere, atque ita et hunc deum dicere, cui deo opus est. Si non de mendacio erubescit adulatio ejusmodi, hominem deum appellans, timeat saltem de infausto. Maledictum est ante apotheosin deum Caesarem nuncupare.
pass_a_gloss: Augustus, the founder of the empire, did not even want to be called lord, for this is also a surname of God. I will call the emperor lord plainly, but in the common manner, and when I am not forced to say lord in place of God. Meanwhile, I am free from him; for my Lord is one, God omnipotent and eternal, who is also the Lord of him. He who is the father of the country, is in this manner lord. But the name of piety is more pleasing than that of power; even families are more often called fathers than lords. So far is it from the case, that the emperor ought to be called God, that it cannot be believed, not only a most shameful, but also a pernicious flattery; as if, having an emperor, you were to call another, would you not incur a great and inexorable offense against him whom you have, and also one to be feared by him himself, whom you called? Be devout to God, who wishes to make Him propitious to the emperor. Cease to worship or believe in another God, and thus also to call this one God, to whom God is needed. If such flattery does not blush at lying, calling a man God, let it at least fear the ill-omened. It is a curse to call Caesar God before his apotheosis.

choices.english: also one to be feared by him himself
rejected: the one you just named becomes the one to fear
choices.why: correct indication of the fear/offense directed toward the actual emperor

pass_b_english: Augustus, the empire's founder, refused even the title 'lord,' because that name belongs to God. I will call the emperor 'lord' plainly enough, but only in the ordinary sense, and only when I am not forced to use it as a substitute for God. As it stands, I am free of him; my Lord is one, the almighty and eternal God, who is also his Lord. The father of the country is lord in that sense alone. Yet the name of piety is more pleasing than the name of power; even in households people are called fathers more often than lords. It is as far from the truth that the emperor ought to be called God as it is impossible to believe such a thing is not merely a shameful but a deadly flattery. It is as if, having an emperor, you were to call another man by that title; would you not incur a great and inexorable offense against the one you actually have, and also make the one you named an object of fear even to himself? Be devout toward God if you want Him propitious to the emperor. Stop worshiping or believing in another God, and so cease calling this man God, a man who himself needs God. If flattery of this sort does not blush at the lie of calling a man God, let it at least fear the ill omen. It is a curse to call Caesar God before his apotheosis.

review.notes: Pass A contains a significant mistranslation of the clause 'Qui pater patriae est, quomodo dominus est.' Pass A translates this as 'He who is the father of the country, is in this manner lord,' which is a nonsensical rendering of the Latin. The Latin 'quomodo' here functions as a rhetorical question or a way of asking 'how [can he be] lord?' (implying he cannot be). Pass B attempts to fix this with 'The father of the country is lord in that sense alone,' but this is an interpretive addition not present in the Latin. Furthermore, Pass A's translation of 'ut dominum dei vice dicam' as 'when I am not forced to say lord in place of God' is slightly awkward compared to the Latin 'vice' (in place of/as a substitute for), though the primary failure is the 'quomodo' clause.
reasons: Pass A translates 'Qui pater patriae est, quomodo dominus est' as 'He who is the father of the country, is in this manner lord,' which fails to capture the interrogative/rhetorical sense of 'quomodo' (how/in what way) and results in a sentence that does not follow the logic of the argument.
